currentContext.expansion: Arvind's expansion in FY26 ran on two tracks. Own capital was deliberately concentrated on India: the Company states it invested approximately Rs 486 crores in growth capex during the year while reducing net debt, under an explicitly 'investment-light' global model that focuses proprietary investment on India-based capacity expansion, technology and Advanced Materials rather than large offshore plants. That India spend showed up as capability rather than headline greenfield capacity - commissioned hybrid captive power capacity in partnership with Torrent Power taking captive energy sourcing to 60%, operationalising India's first supercritical CO2 waterless dyeing facility, launching India's first industrial-scale torrefaction project with Peak Venture, and building a physical demonstration facility in Gujarat under the Future Forward Factories initiative with Fashion for Good. Offshore, the model is partnership-led: a denim plant in Bangladesh held in a joint venture arrangement since 2010 with Bangladesh partnerships further expanded in FY26 in denim and fashion textiles; expanded Egypt partnerships in denim and fashion textiles for EU-preferential access and MENA reach; and, in May 2026, the launch of Arvind Atelier FZC, a wholly owned UAE subsidiary in the Sharjah Airport International Free Zone, alongside a dedicated Design Hub in London positioned for the India-UK FTA. The single largest inorganic step was the announced acquisition on May 06, 2026 of a ~61% controlling stake in U.S.-based Dalco GFT through wholly owned subsidiary Arvind Advanced Materials Limited (AAML), giving AAML a manufacturing base inside the US, a 'Made in USA' positioning that eliminates tariff exposure, and access to an addressable market estimated at USD 2.5 billion across industrial applications, filtration, mobility and protective materials; Dalco GFT carries a revenue base of ~US$100 million with ~17% EBITDA margins and ~40% ROCE, and the transaction is stated to be margin and EPS accretive from the first year. Underlying output moved with this footprint: denim volumes reached 60 million metres (up 15%), woven fabric volume hit an all-time high of 136 million metres and garmenting delivered 42 million pieces, while management notes demand from UK and European buyers is exceeding Arvind's current supply capacity. AAML has been assigned a credit rating of AA with a stable outlook. Process-side expansion is described as debottlenecking and capacity enhancement where required rather than as a named greenfield project pipeline, and no rupee capex plan for a future year is disclosed in this bundle.

risks.note: Named the Company's first key risk. Trade policy shifts, tariff movements and geopolitical developments affect sourcing decisions, customer negotiations, margins and export competitiveness; the stated potential impact is margin pressure, delayed sourcing decisions, cost-sharing requests from customers and uncertainty in export demand. FY26 made this concrete - US tariffs on Indian goods went from 10% in April 2025 to a 50% peak by August 2025 before the February 2026 interim framework cut them to 18%. Mitigation rests on a diversified business model, integrated supply chain, customer relationships and cost optimisation.

Volatility in cotton, specialty fibres and yarns, glass roving, specialty chemicals and resins raises input costs and directly hits profitability. Many Advanced Materials inputs correlate with crude oil, so crude volatility can weaken AMD margins specifically. The cotton MSP was raised up to 11.84% for the 2025-26 season and has roughly doubled over twelve years, cascading cost pressure through the value chain. Managed through price monitoring, inventory management, responsive procurement and contractual pass-through to clients - pass-through that is not guaranteed.

risks.risk: Export-demand compression and concentration in US/European markets
risks.note: The majority of the Company's business is export-oriented. Geopolitical turmoil, global slowdown, high inflation and recession threat in key markets like the US and Europe have already slowed the export market, and demand compression could reduce the export business. Management notes the US/EU macro environment has begun improving but that export demand remains uncertain, with the domestic market as the partial offset. Geographical concentration is also carried on the Company's own strategic risk register.

A significant portion of revenue is in foreign currency while a major part of costs is in Indian Rupees, so any currency movement flows straight to performance. Managed through a periodically reviewed hedging policy, an asset-liability offset approach under which only the net position is hedged, and forward contracts and FX options - which limits but does not eliminate translation and transaction exposure.

risks.risk: Logistics and supply-chain disruption, including supplier concentration
risks.note: Because the business is export-led and dependent on the supply chain to move finished product, disruptions, rising container shipping costs, capacity availability and delays pose severe challenges; inadequate and inefficient logistics within India add delay and cost on top. The Company separately identifies textile value-chain exposure to raw material availability, cotton-growing conditions, trade restrictions and supplier concentration, with the impact stated as input cost volatility, sourcing disruption, production planning difficulty and customer fulfilment risk.

risks.risk: Continuing losses in a few subsidiaries
risks.note: Some subsidiaries are yet to become profitable and others have not shown consistent year-on-year bottom-line improvement, and their subdued performance has negatively impacted consolidated profits. This is a structural drag on the consolidated entity rather than a one-off; the stated remedy is a plan to rationalise capital allocation among the underperforming subsidiaries, which is an intent rather than a completed action.

risks.risk: Water stress in a water-intensive manufacturing base
risks.note: Water is a critical input for textile dyeing and processing and a shared resource with communities, so water stress can hit operating continuity, cost, compliance and stakeholder relationships - the stated impact being reduced production flexibility, higher operating cost, regulatory scrutiny and reputational risk. Customers have made their own water-reduction commitments, making Arvind's water performance a commercial as well as an operational exposure. Mitigation includes Zero Liquid Discharge infrastructure, recycling and reuse, moving away from fresh water sources, supplier water-risk assessment and GWICA collaboration.

risks.risk: Climate physical and transition risk across the fibre-to-fabric chain
risks.note: Assessed against TCFD recommendations across short, medium and long horizons. Physical risks - floods, droughts, heatwaves - can damage assets, disrupt operations and raise costs, and matter disproportionately because the business is tied to cotton-growing ecosystems that are exposed to extreme weather, soil health pressure and freshwater scarcity. Transition risks span policy change, emission reporting, carbon-related costs, technology shifts and rising customer expectations on traceability and sustainable raw materials; the medium-term register explicitly names regulatory change, traceability expectations, sourcing shifts, energy transition and customer consolidation. Rising sustainability compliance cost is separately flagged as a threat that raises production expense.

thesis: Arvind, via subsidiary **AAML**, has acquired **61% of Dalco-GFT** — a ~4-decade-old (est. 1988) US needle-punch nonwovens maker with 2 plants (South Carolina & North Carolina), at **EV of $136mn (7.75x CY25 reported EBITDA)**. This is a strategic step to make Arvind's Advanced Materials Division (AMD) **truly global**, in the **exact same needle-punch-nonwoven technology platform** Arvind already runs in India for filtration. Deal is **margin-accretive and EPS-accretive at Arvind consolidated level** from day one. Target has 17% EBITDA margin, ~40% pre-acquisition RoCE, 10% historical growth — Arvind aims to lift growth to **mid-teens (~15%)** by adding capacity in underpenetrated segments (geotextiles, roofing, flooring) while retaining the entire founder-led management (who roll over ~16-17% equity). Low-touch integration model; founder/team stay 2-4 years via staggered buyout tranches.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Arvind manufactures denim, woven fabrics, knits and finished garments on an integrated yarn-to-finished-goods platform, and separately makes specialised advanced and technical materials through its wholly owned subsidiary Arvind Advanced Materials Limited (AAML). It sells to global apparel brands and retailers across the US, UK, EU and MENA markets as well as the Indian domestic market, and to industrial end-users such as automotive OEMs and infrastructure contractors through Advanced Materials. The Company pairs India-based owned capacity with an explicitly investment-light partnership and joint-venture footprint in Bangladesh, Egypt, the UAE and the United States.

- TAM cited: **$2.5bn across all segments** (Satya); "in the billions" (Punit).

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL)
guidance.body:
- **Dalco-GFT (AMD-US) growth:** target **mid-teens (~15%)** revenue vs historical ~10% — driven by capacity adds + underpenetrated segments (geotextiles, roofing, flooring). Mayank Tiwari framed it as "10–12% revenue growth and mid-teens margin." Punit: US entity grows slightly slower than India entity.
- **AMD division overall:** **20%+ growth aspiration**; India AMD targeted **high-teens to 20%+** (prior 18-20% guidance broadly reaffirmed; not revised down by this deal).
- **Margin:** maintain ~17% (high-teens); possible expansion via operating leverage as scale builds. "Focus is on growth, maintain margins."
- **Capacity / lines:** $5mn ≈ one new line; ~$5mn capex/yr (could be $8mn in a year then pause); capacity NOT a growth constraint — room for 3 more lines in existing 2 plants, enough for ~2+ years. Capex plan to be finalized in 3-4 months.
- **AMD scale-up:** phased — Phase 1 (next ~1.5-2 yrs) = grow US asset base/utilization; Phase 2 = bring tech to India (~2.5 yrs out), filtration expansion in US, cross-sell via sales channels.
- **Consolidation:** from deal close (bought "yesterday"); ~2 months flow into Q1 FY27 console; full financials of Dalco-GFT at Q1 FY27 results.

growth_optionality.title: Growth / optionality (AMD high-margin, China+1, exports)
growth_optionality.body:
- **Immediate (Phase 1):** lift US utilization (85%→90%+) + add lines → mid-teens growth; gain share in geotextiles/roofing/flooring.
- **Second/third-order synergies:** bring nonwoven tech to India (Indian market smaller now but "going to be very large"); take Arvind India products to US on same platform; expand **filtration** in US (large market, Arvind underrepresented); cross-sell via combined sales channels.
- **China+1 / localization:** product must be made close to consumption ("you are shipping air" — high-loft material, ~500-700 mile radius); US-domestic supply de-risks geopolitical exposure; eventual Mexico/Texas expansion possible once current plants exhausted.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management states demand for Textiles and Advanced Materials continues to remain resilient with major sourcing destinations largely stable, despite an uncertain global trade environment
- The current order book is at healthy levels supported by a robust inquiry pipeline for the upcoming season - the explicit basis for management's double-digit growth expectation
- Verticalisation is the named driver of higher denim volumes: customers are diversifying vendor bases and increasingly prefer integrated one-stop solutions to optimise cost, lead time and supply-chain efficiency
- Garment revenue growth is attributed to higher demand in knitwear and denim
- Input costs across product lines have risen sharply and could pressure margins in H1, with margin recovery expected in H2 subject to easing geopolitical tensions
- Cotton prices rose from the start of calendar 2026 but market projections indicate range-bound prices through the year on improved global supply-demand balance and a more stable macro outlook; MSP was raised up to 11.84% for the 2025-26 season, cascading cost pressure through the textile value chain
- Dyes and chemicals, especially freight-linked ones, began softening in H2FY26, while AMD inputs (specialty yarns, glass rovings, resin systems, chemicals) stayed range bound
- Trade policy is the dominant swing factor: US tariffs on Indian goods escalated from 10% to a 50% peak during FY26 before the February 2026 India-US Interim Trade Framework cut them to 18%, unlocking a USD ~114 billion addressable US market
- India-UK CETA (concluded May 2025) eliminates tariffs on 99% of Indian exports to the UK, giving Indian exporters an approximately 10% cost advantage over regional competitors; an India-EU FTA, if concluded, could render 70-75% of India's textile exports effectively duty-free globally
- US tariff volatility accelerated 'China-plus-one' and 'Bangladesh-plus-one' sourcing by global brands, narrowing and in some categories reversing India's disadvantage versus Bangladesh and Vietnam
- Demand from UK and European buyers is reported to be exceeding Arvind's current supply capacity, creating immediate commercial opportunity for the London Design Hub from Day 1
- The Dalco-GFT acquisition opens an addressable market estimated at USD 2.5 billion across industrial applications, filtration, mobility and protective materials, with domestic-content preference from US automotive OEMs and infrastructure contractors
- Structural shift toward man-made fibres (MMFs are ~77% of global fibre usage) supported by the extended PLI Scheme for Textiles and the National Fibre Scheme announced in Union Budget 2026-27
- Policy tailwinds for domestic manufacturing: import duty on shuttle-less Rapier and Air Jet looms cut from 7.5% to nil, and a higher basic customs duty on knitted fabrics protecting domestic producers and encouraging higher capacity utilisation
- Domestic demand tailwind from a growing middle class, e-commerce growth and Gen Z consumption; the Indian textile and apparel market is projected to grow at a 10% CAGR to USD 350 billion by 2030
- Management remains mindful of potential demand volatility in H2 driven by elevated inflationary pressures and global uncertainties that may hit discretionary consumption
- Threats flagged include India's weak export competitiveness versus China, Vietnam and Bangladesh; fragmented cotton supply and costlier MMF than China; burdensome export procedures; rising sustainability compliance costs; and labour instability from rising minimum wages, high attrition and migrant worker challenges
- Named enterprise risks: raw material price volatility (including AMD inputs correlating with crude oil), economic/export demand compression from US and Europe slowdown, and exchange-rate volatility given revenue is largely in foreign currency against Rupee costs, managed via a periodically reviewed hedging policy and asset-liability offset
- The current order book is at healthy levels, supported by a robust inquiry pipeline for the upcoming season - this is the stated basis for the double-digit growth expectation
- Demand from UK and European buyers is reported to be exceeding Arvind's current supply capacity, creating immediate commercial opportunity from Day 1 of the London Design Hub's operations

margins.title: Margins & cost
margins.body:
- Dalco EBITDA margin ~17% (best-in-class for needle-punch nonwoven / auto); cost-per-kg best-in-class due to operating efficiency. Highly automated → headcount won't rise much; only small BD/customer-service team additions.
- **RM:** mostly polymers / staple fiber (polyester / polypropylene), petroleum-linked → some inflation; **65-70% sourced locally in US**, rest Korea/Vietnam. Polymer prices up but "manageable"; cost increases being passed on; flagged war/oil situation as watch-item.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Deal funded **entirely by debt** (to use tax shields in both geographies): **$50mn at US/Dalco level** (was $15mn → +$35mn) and **$60mn at AAML/India level** = ~$110mn raised; outlay ~$84-85mn for ~70% economic interest; existing shareholders also participate in debt. Net debt in target $16-17mn.
- **Cost of debt:** US ~5.5% (SOFR-linked); AAML ~6%. 5-year loan.
- **Stated intent:** Group philosophy = no long-term debt on books; aim to **wind down acquisition debt over ~2 years** via cash flows. Post-acq ratios within existing covenants; expected to improve in 12 months.
- **Staggered buyout:** residual equity bought in 2 tranches (2 yrs and 4 yrs); mgmt skews toward 4-yr; PE sponsor exits sooner; founder holds ~16-17% through 4 yrs. Fresh long-term performance-linked incentives reset for mgmt.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Arvind's expansion in FY26 ran on two tracks. Own capital was deliberately concentrated on India: the Company states it invested approximately Rs 486 crores in growth capex during the year while reducing net debt, under an explicitly 'investment-light' global model that focuses proprietary investment on India-based capacity expansion, technology and Advanced Materials rather than large offshore plants. That India spend showed up as capability rather than headline greenfield capacity - commissioned hybrid captive power capacity in partnership with Torrent Power taking captive energy sourcing to 60%, operationalising India's first supercritical CO2 waterless dyeing facility, launching India's first industrial-scale torrefaction project with Peak Venture, and building a physical demonstration facility in Gujarat under the Future Forward Factories initiative with Fashion for Good. Offshore, the model is partnership-led: a denim plant in Bangladesh held in a joint venture arrangement since 2010 with Bangladesh partnerships further expanded in FY26 in denim and fashion textiles; expanded Egypt partnerships in denim and fashion textiles for EU-preferential access and MENA reach; and, in May 2026, the launch of Arvind Atelier FZC, a wholly owned UAE subsidiary in the Sharjah Airport International Free Zone, alongside a dedicated Design Hub in London positioned for the India-UK FTA. The single largest inorganic step was the announced acquisition on May 06, 2026 of a ~61% controlling stake in U.S.-based Dalco GFT through wholly owned subsidiary Arvind Advanced Materials Limited (AAML), giving AAML a manufacturing base inside the US, a 'Made in USA' positioning that eliminates tariff exposure, and access to an addressable market estimated at USD 2.5 billion across industrial applications, filtration, mobility and protective materials; Dalco GFT carries a revenue base of ~US$100 million with ~17% EBITDA margins and ~40% ROCE, and the transaction is stated to be margin and EPS accretive from the first year. Underlying output moved with this footprint: denim volumes reached 60 million metres (up 15%), woven fabric volume hit an all-time high of 136 million metres and garmenting delivered 42 million pieces, while management notes demand from UK and European buyers is exceeding Arvind's current supply capacity. AAML has been assigned a credit rating of AA with a stable outlook. Process-side expansion is described as debottlenecking and capacity enhancement where required rather than as a named greenfield project pipeline, and no rupee capex plan for a future year is disclosed in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management tone
management_tone.body: Very confident / enthusiastic. Punit "extraordinarily excited"; repeatedly stressed quality of the founder-led team, philosophical/chemistry alignment, "fair value" paid via competitive process, and EPS/margin accretion. Reiterated AMD's global ambition and 20%+ growth aspiration. Transparent on deal mechanics but deferred goodwill/financial-statement detail to Q1 FY27.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Vertical integration from yarn to finished goods across denim, woven, knits and garmenting, giving a fabric-to-garment proposition that global customers increasingly want
- Scale, with an all-time-high woven fabric volume of 136 million metres, denim volume of 60 million metres and 42 million garment pieces in FY26
- Diversified customer portfolio and geographic footprint, which management credits for margin resilience through the FY26 tariff shock
- Investment-light global model - partnerships and JVs in Bangladesh and Egypt, a UAE subsidiary and a London design hub - that captures supply-chain diversification demand without heavy offshore capital
- Made in USA positioning through the Dalco-GFT acquisition, eliminating tariff exposure and meeting domestic-content preferences of US automotive OEMs and infrastructure contractors
- Sustainability leadership used as a commercial differentiator: first textile mill globally in ZDHC, SBTi-approved targets, India's first supercritical CO2 dyeing facility, and an S&P Global CSA score of 74 against a global industry average of 31
- Technology and process depth - SAP ERP, IoT-enabled process monitoring, advanced analytics, traceability systems and laboratory instrumentation supporting chemical compliance
- Intellectual capital base of domain knowledge, patents, products, technology partnerships and R&D capability supporting differentiation beyond scale
- Structured Supplier Sustainability Assessment programme giving the supply-chain transparency and risk mitigation that global brands demand

risks.title: Risks
risks.body:
- **US demand / tariff:** auto end-market cyclical (auto only 3-4% base growth); however US auto described as "protected" from China; deal is US-domestic so direct US-import-tariff exposure limited — but US macro/demand and infrastructure-bill execution dependence remain.
- **Commodity:** polymer/petroleum-linked RM inflation; oil/war escalation risk (partly passed through).
- **Execution / integration:** classic overseas-acquisition risk; mitigated by low-touch model, retained team, same tech platform. Leverage flagged by analysts as "on the higher side" (debt-to-EBITDA) — mgmt commits to rapid paydown.
- Goodwill / full balance-sheet detail NOT yet disclosed → transparency gap until Q1 FY27.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious insights
non_obvious.body:
- Deal is **margin AND EPS accretive day one** — rare for a debt-funded cross-border buy.
- **"Shipping air"** logistics constraint (high-loft nonwoven, 500-700 mile radius) is structurally why this can't be relocated to India — protects US plants and forces local-for-local, a moat.
- Platform **fungibility** across auto/geotextile/roofing/flooring is the real risk-containment mechanism across cycles (Mayank Tiwari).
- 85-88% **sole-sourced** auto spec-ins + 5-7 yr platform life = very sticky, annuity-like revenue.
- Pre-acquisition **40% RoCE** target was efficiency-optimized by PE owner; Arvind's thesis is to trade some of that for growth (capacity adds) without losing margin.
- Filtration in US is an under-exploited optionality Arvind already has India capability for.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Verticalisation - converting a growing proportion of own fabric volumes into garments by transforming select fabric customers into vertically integrated customers, offering an integrated one-stop fabric-to-garment solution that cuts customer cost, lead time and supply-chain complexity
- Investment-light global expansion - partnership, JV and sourcing alliances in Bangladesh and Egypt plus the Arvind Atelier FZC UAE subsidiary and London Design Hub, deliberately avoiding large proprietary offshore capital while concentrating own capital on India capacity, technology and Advanced …

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries (✅ / ⭐ may be empty)
challenges.body:
- ✅ **Arvind / AAML** — primary beneficiary: instant global scale in a tech it knows, accretive deal, high-margin/high-RoCE asset, US Infrastructure Bill geotextile tailwind.
- ⭐ India technical-textile/nonwoven peers — read-through that US needle-punch-nonwoven assets command ~7.75x EBITDA and that domestic technical-textile capability is being globalized (sector re-rating signal).
- Auto Tier-1 NVH supply chain (US) — Arvind now a deeper Tier-2 participant.
